solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Father is back — foul, debauched man grabbing southern explorer (3,7,5)

indicators.note: 'back' turns FR and IS round to read SIRF
RANCID grabs the S, holding it inside

blocks.note: a rake is a debauched man

annotation.surface: An indignant report that a priest has returned, and a foul, debauched man has made off with an explorer from the south.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash splits the clue into scandalised sentences, but it is all one charade; only 'explorer' at the very end defines.
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake was the Elizabethan explorer who sailed round the world.

clue.text: Help gullible chap to be heard (7)

indicators.note: the answer is what a listener hears, not what is written

blocks.note: a sucker is a gullible chap

annotation.surface: A plea for help from a gullible man who wants to be listened to.
annotation.walkthrough: In most British accents SUCCOUR and SUCKER sound identical.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain but old-fashioned synonym: succour is help given in time of need, as a noun or a verb.

clue.text: Dance graduate supporting group periodically (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue the graduate sits underneath, holding up the other piece
take every other letter of 'group'

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of gRoUp
an MBA is a business graduate

annotation.surface: A dance graduate who backs some group now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dance graduate' reads as one person, a trained dancer; the definition is 'Dance' alone, and the graduate is an MBA, a business degree.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the rumba, of Cuban origin, is one of the standard Latin ballroom dances.

clue.text: Ruler and a rogue clergyman (5,4)

indicators.note: rogue letters are unruly ones, so the fodder is rearranged

annotation.surface: A monarch and some rogue priest, a medieval odd couple.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' reads as the definition at the start; it is fodder, and the definition is the clergyman at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A rural dean is a Church of England clergyman supervising a group of parishes.

clue.text: Just robbed of house and home (4)

indicators.note: something robbed of a thing no longer has it, so HONEST is left without HO

blocks.note: HO is the abbreviation for house

annotation.surface: Someone upright has been burgled of house and home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'House and home' reads as a stock phrase, but only 'home' defines; 'house' is the HO taken away.
annotation.definitionFit: A nest is a bird's home, and by extension anyone's.

clue.text: The author had time to welcome flipping daft poet (8)

indicators.note: ID and T take the other piece in between them
SILLY is flipped end to end

blocks.note: the setter would say I'd = I had

annotation.surface: The setter confesses to having had time to host a hopelessly daft poet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The author' is the setter speaking of himself, so the words become I'D. 'Flipping' pretends to be a mild British curse.
annotation.definitionFit: An idyllist is a poet who writes idylls, short pastoral poems.

clue.text: Physicist cut dreadful article on speed of light (5)

indicators.note: DIRE is cut short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: c is the physicists' symbol for the speed of light

annotation.surface: A physicist edits out a dreadful article about the speed of light.
annotation.walkthrough: The physics surface is apt: Dirac was a physicist, and c really is his field's symbol for light speed.
annotation.definitionFit: Paul Dirac was a British theoretical physicist, a founder of quantum mechanics.

clue.text: Instrument one cooler chain stocks (9)

indicators.note: CORDON stocks the I, keeping it inside

blocks.note: a cordon is a chain of police or guards

annotation.surface: A shop chain stocks an instrument and a cooler.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' looks like a comparative adjective or a drinks box; it is air conditioning. 'Chain stocks' pretends to be a shop's inventory.
annotation.definitionFit: An accordion is a bellows-driven musical instrument.

clue.text: US lawman left university, ultimately inventing anti-listening device (7)

indicators.note: take the last letter of 'inventing'

blocks.note: Wyatt Earp, the Wild West marshal

annotation.surface: A US lawman quit university to invent a device that defeats eavesdropping.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left university' reads as dropping out, but it is simply L and U side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: An earplug stops you hearing, so it is a device against listening.

clue.text: Appeared reckless before Yankee not wanting to be shot (6-3)

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Someone turned up recklessly ahead of an American who is anxious not to be shot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shot' sounds like gunfire in this surface; the answer means shot by a camera.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone camera-shy dislikes being photographed, that is, shot.

clue.text: Snake right next to tree (5)

indicators.note: R is placed beside the tree

annotation.surface: A snake lies just by a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: Acer, the botanical name for maples, is a crossword regular among trees, as are ASH, ELM and YEW.
annotation.definitionFit: Racers are fast North American snakes.

clue.text: Person relaying prophecy heading off in boat (6)

indicators.note: the boat's first letter comes off

blocks.note: a coracle is a small round boat; drop its C

annotation.surface: A prophet sets off in a boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as setting out on a journey; here it means losing the head letter.
annotation.definitionFit: An oracle, like the one at Delphi, passed on prophecies from the gods.

clue.text: Learning chemistry, leaving short of content about compound (8)

indicators.note: both words lose their insides, keeping only the outer letters
the whole string is turned round

annotation.surface: A student drops chemistry, wanting for content, and it concerns some compound.
annotation.walkthrough: LORECYLG turned round reads GLYCEROL. 'Chemistry' and 'compound' sit in the surface to make the clue look like a science lesson.
annotation.definitionFit: Glycerol (glycerine) is a chemical compound, a simple alcohol.

clue.text: Epitaph by an admirable person from Australia (6)

blocks.note: RIP, rest in peace, is the standard epitaph

annotation.surface: A gravestone inscription for some splendid Australian.
annotation.walkthrough: Ripper is Australian slang for something or someone excellent; 'from Australia' flags the slang.
annotation.definitionFit: In Australian English, a ripper is a first-rate person or thing.

clue.text: Stunted cyberbully roughly put into standard police vehicle (6,3)

indicators.note: TROLL is cut short, losing its last letter
something put into a container ends up inside it, so TROL and CA go inside PAR

blocks.note: a troll is an online bully; stunted, it loses an L
par = standard, as in 'up to par'

annotation.surface: A crude online bully gets locked in the back of a squad car.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' pretends to be an adverb for 'put'; it is CA, the abbreviation for circa. 'Standard' looks like an adjective for the vehicle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the police send cars out on patrol, and 'patrol car' is the standard name for them.

clue.text: Forcefully seizing king, entering on horseback with guards (8)

indicators.note: a thing entering a place goes inside it, so R goes into UP
USING guards URP, holding it inside

blocks.note: a jockey who is 'up' is riding
using = with, as in 'with a spoon'

annotation.surface: A mounted guard party seizes a king by force.
annotation.walkthrough: The king and guards picture a coup, which is exactly what usurping is. UP for riding is racing jargon: 'Dettori is up'.
annotation.definitionFit: Usurping is seizing power or a throne by force.

clue.text: Reject authority of pirate due to wind (9)

indicators.note: letters that wind about are twisted into a new order

annotation.surface: A pirate throws off his captain's authority because of the wind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Due to wind' reads as 'because of the weather'; 'due' is fodder and 'wind' is the verb, rhyming with 'find'.
annotation.definitionFit: To repudiate is to refuse to accept or recognise, as with a debt or authority.

clue.text: Singer due to receive millions here stripped (8)

indicators.note: HERE loses its outer letters

blocks.note: in for = due to receive, as in 'in for a treat'

annotation.surface: A singer is set to rake in millions here, then gets stripped of it.
annotation.walkthrough: A singer here is someone who 'sings' to the police, not a vocalist.
annotation.definitionFit: Underworld slang says an informer 'sings', giving information to the police.

clue.text: Adjusting giant nut carelessly (8)

indicators.note: the letters are thrown together carelessly, out of order

annotation.surface: A mechanic sloppily adjusts a huge nut.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Adjusting' a mechanic's word, turning a spanner; the answer is adjusting in the sense of tuning or bringing into harmony.
annotation.definitionFit: Attuning is adjusting something so it is in tune or in harmony.

clue.text: Don’t booze with sailors — you shouldn’t have contents of pint (7)

indicators.note: take only what is inside 'pint'

blocks.note: ta = thanks, the polite reply 'you shouldn't have'

annotation.surface: A friend refuses a pint in the sailors' bar: you really should not have one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' is what you say when given a present, so it stands for TA, British for thanks.
annotation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain from drinking alcohol.

clue.text: Somewhat hope nuptials become more lively (4,2)

indicators.note: only some of the words are used, so the answer is part of them

annotation.surface: A modest wish that the wedding livens up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat hope' reads as a hesitant wish; 'somewhat' means only part of the letters are used, and the answer spans the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A game or party that opens up becomes freer and more lively.

clue.text: Warn of combining wine and Pernod on a regular basis (7)

indicators.note: take the regularly spaced letters of 'Pernod'

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of pErNoD

annotation.surface: A health warning against mixing wine and Pernod as a habit.
annotation.walkthrough: Pernod is a French aniseed spirit; its alternate letters, not its flavour, are used.
annotation.definitionFit: To portend is to warn of, or be an omen of, something to come.

clue.text: Violent downpours knocking out uranium plant (8)

indicators.note: the letters are thrown about violently
the U is knocked out of the fodder first

blocks.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium; it comes out

annotation.surface: Torrential rain has wrecked a nuclear power plant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant' pretends to be an industrial site, helped by 'uranium'; it is a flower.
annotation.definitionFit: The snowdrop is a small white-flowered plant blooming in late winter.

clue.text: Diamonds ground without resistance in the end (5)

indicators.note: to go without something is to lack it, so EARTH is left lacking its R

blocks.note: R is the physics symbol for resistance; it is removed

annotation.surface: Diamonds are eventually ground down, having no resistance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like the past tense of grind; it is the noun, earth.
annotation.definitionFit: Death is the end of life, so 'the end' works as a euphemism.

clue.text: One who loves trouble starts to rewatch Easy Rider (6)

indicators.note: take the first letter of each following word

annotation.surface: A film fan who likes a bit of trouble puts on Easy Rider again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loves trouble' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'loves'. Easy Rider is the 1969 biker film.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to adore is to love deeply, so an adorer is a devoted lover or fan.

clue.text: Sent up character drinking orange juice and wine (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending AIR up the column makes it read RIA
whoever is drinking takes the drink inside, so RIA takes OJ into itself

blocks.note: an air is a character or manner, as in 'an air of calm'
OJ is the usual abbreviation for orange juice

annotation.surface: A character who was mocked is drinking orange juice and wine.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinks are a smoke screen: OJ is the only juice used, and the wine is the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Rioja is a red wine from the Rioja region of Spain.

clue.text: European travel company’s case (4)

blocks.note: TUI is a big European travel company

annotation.surface: A suitcase belonging to a European tour operator.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive; it is 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles or toiletries.

clue.text: Capital account raid ignored by papers (5)

indicators.note: the papers, ID, are left out of RAID

blocks.note: acc. is the abbreviation for account
the word itself, before the deletion
ID papers are identity documents; they come out

annotation.surface: A raid on a capital account is ignored by the newspapers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital account' is a banking term, which hides the city; 'papers' reads as newspapers, not identity documents.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Accra is one capital city among many, the capital of Ghana.

clue.text: Assistance to get off horse? (9)

blocks.note: the surface reading: help climbing down from a horse, such as a mounting block or a groom's hand
the meant reading: horse is drug slang for heroin, so this is a treatment that helps an addict quit

annotation.surface: A question about help dismounting a horse.
annotation.walkthrough: Horse is slang for heroin, so getting off horse means quitting heroin, and methadone is the drug used to do it.
annotation.definitionFit: Methadone is a synthetic opioid prescribed to help heroin addicts withdraw.

clue.text: Revolutionary capitalised in expanding part of UK (8,7)

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so IN becomes NI
written in capitals, NI becomes the abbreviation N.I.
an abbreviation is expanded by writing it out in full

blocks.note: IN turned round is NI; in capitals, N.I. is a standard abbreviation, and expanding it means writing it out in full

annotation.surface: Some revolutionary has made money in a growing corner of the United Kingdom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capitalised' reads as financed and 'Revolutionary' as a rebel, but both work on the tiny word 'in', which becomes N.I. and is then spelt out.
annotation.definitionFit: Northern Ireland is one of the four nations of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
